title: Claude Opus 5.5 for Revit and AutoCAD: A Louver That Fits Two Sizes
summary: Claude Opus 5.5 is in ArchiLabs Desktop. See its parametric CAD benchmark results and how to build a Revit louver family or AutoCAD block in two sizes.
body_markdown:
Suppose the first louver fits, and the mechanical engineer sends a wider opening for the room next door. Scale up the first louver and the frame gets thicker, too. Stretch just the right edge and the blades may stop short of the frame. What looked like a perfectly good model at one size has just told you how it was built.


**Claude Opus 5.5 is available in ArchiLabs Desktop for Revit and AutoCAD work.** Anthropic released it on September 22, 2026. If you build families or reusable details, one of the most informative results since that release comes from a CAD test that scored drawing reconstruction and follow-up edits as separate tasks.[Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-opus-5-5)


## What the Claude Opus 5.5 CAD benchmark says about the second edit


In Parametric CAD Bench v3, agents worked in FreeCAD on 100 tasks. On 40 of them, the agent received an engineering drawing and had to reconstruct the part. On another 30, it had to build a part from a written brief and then change it. The researchers checked how closely the resulting file matched the target shape and specifications. A partly correct model could earn partial credit.[Parametric CAD Bench v3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.02659)


With Claude Code at maximum effort, Opus 5.5 earned **84.66% mean reward on drawing-to-CAD tasks** and **39.69% on create-and-edit tasks** in the September 24 results. These were different sets of parts. They give us a good reason to ask two questions of a new family. Does it match the first drawing? And when the width changes, which pieces follow?[Results by task and model configuration](https://cadbench.ai/leaderboard)


## Claude Opus 5.5 for Revit families in ArchiLabs Desktop


For the louver, give Opus the manufacturer’s front view and section in Desktop. The front view establishes the outline. The section shows the frame depth and how the blades sit inside it. If the catalog lists a nominal opening width and a smaller outside frame width, label both. The difference matters to the person laying out the opening.


> Build a Revit louver family from these two catalog sizes. Use the outside frame width for the family width. Both sizes have the same height, frame profile, and blade spacing. Make the blades follow the clear width between the side frames. Flag any missing dimension.


Load the two sizes side by side. In elevation, the wider one should gain blade length while the side frames keep their catalog face width. Cut a section through each to check frame depth. If the front view looks right but the section has stretched, you now know exactly what to ask Opus to fix. You can see Desktop create and place a native equipment family from a manufacturer’s PDF in our recorded Revit demo.[Watch the ArchiLabs Desktop family demo](https://archilabs.ai/desktop)


## Claude Opus 5.5 for AutoCAD louver details


If the deliverable is a DWG, the same design intent leads to a different request. Select the existing louver block in Desktop and identify the jamb your team dimensions from. Ask Opus to make the second size as a separate block definition, keep that jamb at the insertion point, and update the overall width dimension. The first size may already appear on a dozen sheets.


Insert both blocks at the same point in a working detail. The fixed jambs should coincide. The opposite jambs should differ by the change in width, and the side frames should have equal face widths. That overlay takes the ambiguity out of the review. The next time the engineer sends a size, the drafter knows which dimension to change and what the result should look like.
